fields.Front:
Your team uses Claude Code for multi-file refactors that routinely run two to three hours. Engineers currently type the task and let Claude start editing immediately; in about a third of these sessions Claude's approach diverges from what the engineer intended, and they spend 40-plus minutes reverting and re-prompting after the fact.

What working habit would most reduce this cleanup time?

A. Switch the sessions to a larger-context model so Claude retains the engineer's original intent for the full run.
B. Add a CLAUDE.md rule stating that Claude must describe its intended approach before editing any file.
C. Start each refactor in plan mode, read the proposed plan thoroughly, and iterate on it before approving execution.
D. Break every refactor into single-file tasks and dispatch each one to a fresh session.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C targets the root cause: in plan mode Claude researches without editing your source and hands you a plan to review, and iterating on a plan is much faster than letting Claude run and cleaning up afterward — a thorough, actually-read plan means fewer surprises during execution. Option A misdiagnoses the problem; the divergence is a scoping failure, not a context-capacity failure. Option B relies on probabilistic instruction-following and produces no reviewable artifact you can iterate on before code changes. Option D destroys the cross-file context a refactor depends on and multiplies coordination overhead across sessions. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Choose a permission mode — Analyze before you edit with plan mode (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code

fields.Front: Four hours into a Claude Code session, you finished a lengthy debugging detour 90 minutes ago and are now implementing a --version flag. The context window is nearly full. The last time you ran a bare /compact in a similar session, the summary kept the debugging details, dropped the implementation decisions you cared about, and Claude drifted. How should you free up context while keeping Claude on track? A. Run a bare /compact once more; the summarizer automatically weights recent implementation work over older detours. B. Run /compact with instructions that name what to keep, such as /compact Focus on the --version flag implementation. C. Switch to a model with a larger context window and continue the session without compacting, so nothing gets summarized. D. Start a fresh session and re-explain the --version task from scratch, which guarantees a context free of debugging detail.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B uses compaction's steering wheel: anything written after the command shapes what the summary keeps, so the --version work survives and the stale debugging detour is dropped. Option A repeats exactly the failure described — an undirected summary gives you no control over what gets kept. Option C postpones the problem and leaves the irrelevant debugging content in context competing for attention. Option D throws away all accumulated, still-relevant context and costs significant re-explanation time when a directed summary would have preserved it. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Explore the context window — When your context fills up (Claude Code docs) • Commands — All commands (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Manage context aggressively

fields.Front: Fifty minutes into a feature build, you realize Claude committed to the wrong architecture about 20 minutes ago and has since edited nine files on that basis. Engineers on your team usually respond by prompting corrections such as 'undo all of that and go back to the event-based approach', which typically takes another half hour and leaves stray code behind. What is the most reliable way to get both the code and the conversation back on track? A. Send one detailed corrective prompt that asks Claude to revert all of its changes and restates the event-based architecture. B. Use git checkout to restore the nine edited files, then continue working in the existing conversation. C. End the session and start a new one with an empty context so no trace of the wrong architecture can influence Claude. D. Press Esc twice to open the rewind menu and restore code and conversation to the checkpoint before the wrong turn.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D uses what checkpoints are for: every user prompt creates one, and restoring code and conversation together removes both the bad edits and the conversational context that keeps steering Claude toward the abandoned architecture. Option A is the slow pattern the team already suffers from — probabilistic cleanup that leaves strays. Option B rolls back the files but leaves 20 minutes of wrong-architecture discussion in context, so Claude is likely to drift back. Option C discards the 30 minutes of good context that preceded the wrong turn when a checkpoint restore would have kept it. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Checkpointing — Rewind and summarize (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Rewind with checkpoints • Interactive mode — General controls (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your Claude Code session began with 90 minutes of codebase exploration and environment setup before implementation started. You are now deep in implementation, the context window is at 85%, and the recent implementation turns contain decisions Claude must keep in full detail. Which action frees context while preserving the implementation detail? A. Open the rewind menu and choose 'Summarize up to here' at the checkpoint where implementation began. B. Open the rewind menu and choose 'Restore conversation' at the checkpoint where implementation began. C. Run a bare /compact so the entire conversation, setup and implementation alike, is summarized. D. Continue without compacting and rely on the model to attend to recent turns over older ones.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the designed move for a long setup phase: 'Summarize up to here' compresses everything before the chosen checkpoint while keeping everything after it — the implementation turns — intact. Option B does not compress anything; restoring the conversation at that checkpoint deletes the implementation turns you need to keep. Option C summarizes the implementation detail along with the setup, risking exactly the decisions you need verbatim. Option D leaves the window filling toward overflow while 90 minutes of stale setup keeps competing for attention. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Checkpointing — Rewind and summarize (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Manage context aggressively

fields.Front: You want Claude Code to keep working across turns on a billing module until it is genuinely done, rather than stopping the first time it thinks it is finished. A teammate proposes running /goal the billing dashboard looks correct and users are happy with it. What should you tell the teammate? A. The condition is too brief; expand it with a detailed description of the dashboard's intended design so the evaluator has more to compare against. B. Rephrase it as something checkable from Claude's own output, such as /goal all tests in src/billing pass and the type checker reports zero errors. C. A /goal condition can hold only one clause, so split it: run /goal the dashboard looks correct now and handle user satisfaction in a second session. D. Keep the condition, but have Claude report a confidence score at the end of each turn and treat 95% or higher as the signal that the goal is met.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B states the one hard constraint on goals: the evaluator, a small fast model, judges the condition only against what Claude has surfaced in the conversation — it does not run commands or read files itself — so 'done' must be phrased as something Claude's own output can demonstrate, like test results or type-checker output. 'Looks correct and users are happy' produces nothing checkable. Option A adds words without adding verifiability; a longer unverifiable condition is still unverifiable. Option C invents a limit: only one goal is active per session, but a single condition can join several clauses, and splitting this one would not make either half checkable. Option D substitutes self-reported confidence for evidence, and a model's confidence score is not a reliable completion signal. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Keep Claude working toward a goal — Write an effective condition (Claude Code docs) • Keep Claude working toward a goal — How evaluation works (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work

fields.Front: After Claude Code pushes a branch, your team wants the same interactive session to watch the CI run — runs take 10 to 20 minutes — and triage any failures once it finishes. Today engineers sit at the terminal re-asking 'is CI done yet?' every few minutes. Which Claude Code capability fits this job? A. Set /goal CI passes; the goal evaluator will poll the pipeline until the condition is met. B. Add a CLAUDE.md rule instructing Claude to always wait for CI to finish before ending its turn. C. Raise the session's turn budget so Claude keeps retrying the CI status check until the run completes. D. Start a loop that runs a status-check prompt on an interval so Claude acts when the CI state changes.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is what /loop exists for: it re-runs a prompt on a fixed or self-paced interval between turns while the session stays open, which is exactly the shape of polling external state like CI or a deploy and reacting when it changes. Option A misunderstands /goal — its evaluator only judges a completion condition against what Claude has already surfaced in the conversation; it does not run commands or poll external systems. Option B is a probabilistic instruction, and an instruction cannot make a turn wait on an external event. Option C burns turns on blind retries, automating the team's current busywork rather than replacing it with an interval-driven check. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Run prompts on a schedule — Run a prompt repeatedly with /loop (Claude Code docs) • Keep Claude working toward a goal — Compare ways to keep a session running (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Three feature refactors are due this week, so your team runs three concurrent Claude Code sessions against the same repository. In roughly 30% of runs, one session overwrites files another session just edited. Each feature's dev server also needs a git-ignored .env.local file to boot, and security policy forbids committing it. Which TWO changes let the three sessions run in parallel reliably? (Select TWO.) A. Run each session in its own git worktree so every agent works on an independent file tree. B. Serialize the work into a single session and queue the three refactors one after another. C. Add a .worktreeinclude file at the repo root listing .env.local so it is copied into each worktree. D. Commit .env.local to the repository so every checkout automatically includes it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and C. Options A and C are both required. Worktrees (A) end the clobbering: each session gets its own working directory and branch, so edits in one session never touch files in another. But a worktree is a fresh checkout that does not contain git-ignored files, so the dev servers would fail to boot; a .worktreeinclude file (C) lists exactly those files — env files, local config — to copy into each worktree Claude Code creates. Option B eliminates the conflicts by abandoning the parallelism the deadline requires. Option D puts secrets into version control, which policy forbids and which .worktreeinclude makes unnecessary. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Run parallel sessions with worktrees — Copy gitignored files into worktrees (Claude Code docs) • Run parallel sessions with worktrees — Start Claude in a worktree (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions

fields.Front: Your team uses Claude Code on a repository whose project CLAUDE.md contains 'IMPORTANT: never push directly to main.' Over the last month of heavy agent use, Claude pushed to main twice out of roughly 200 sessions, each time triggering an incident review. What is the right fix? A. Move the rule to the first line of CLAUDE.md and repeat it at the bottom, keeping softer conventions there too. B. Add a SessionStart hook that prints the rule to stdout, and keep CLAUDE.md for softer conventions. C. Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks any push to main, and keep CLAUDE.md for softer conventions. D. Add a PostToolUse hook that flags any push to main back to Claude, and keep CLAUDE.md for softer conventions.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C matches the surface to the rule: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforced configuration, and 99% compliance is not good enough for an action with incident-level consequences. A PreToolUse hook is code that runs before the action and blocks it even when Claude tries it — real enforcement instead of a polite request. Option A is an escalation of prompt-only enforcement: it may lower the failure rate but remains probabilistic, and a hard line that must never be crossed cannot depend on instruction-following. Option B uses a real hook event, but SessionStart only adds the rule to context when a session starts, so it is one more instruction Claude can ignore and nothing in it stops a push. Option D puts the check on the wrong side of the action: PostToolUse runs only after the tool call has finished, so the push to main has already happened, and with it the incident. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • How Claude remembers your project — CLAUDE.md vs auto memory (Claude Code docs) • Automate actions with hooks — Block edits to protected files (Claude Code docs) • Hooks reference — PreToolUse decision control (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to 700 lines mixing style conventions, long task-specific reference material, and a rule that Claude must never run destructive database commands against the shared staging environment. Adherence has degraded across the board, and last week Claude ran a destructive command against staging anyway. Which TWO changes most directly address these failures? (Select TWO.) A. Mark every rule in the file IMPORTANT so that none of them is deprioritized when instructions compete for attention. B. Move the destructive-command rule into a PreToolUse hook that blocks matching commands before they run. C. Split the 700 lines across ten files pulled in with @ imports to reduce the context the file consumes. D. Trim the file to the conventions that matter and move task-specific reference material into skills that load on demand.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and D. Options B and D fix the two distinct failures. The staging rule is a hard line, and CLAUDE.md is guidance that Claude can fail to follow; a PreToolUse hook (B) blocks the action deterministically even on runs nobody is watching. The adherence collapse is a length problem: every line competes with every other line for attention, so trimming the file and scoping task-specific material into skills (D) makes the remaining rules more reliably followed. Option A is emphasis inflation — if every rule shouts, nothing stands out. Option C only reorganizes: imports are expanded inline at launch, so everything still loads and the attention competition is unchanged. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — CLAUDE.md vs auto memory (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features

fields.Front: A line in your CLAUDE.md reads 'Follow best practices for API routes.' Code review still flags misplaced route files in about 4 of every 10 Claude-generated PRs, and your own engineers disagree about what the rule actually requires. How should the rule be rewritten? A. Make it specific and checkable, such as 'Put new API routes in src/api/handlers, one file per route.' B. Prefix it with IMPORTANT so it wins the competition for Claude's attention. C. Replace it with a PreToolUse hook that rejects any edit whose diff violates best practices. D. Import the team's full 30-page style guide into CLAUDE.md so best practices are completely defined.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A clears the bar every rule should meet: you can look at the result and immediately tell whether it was followed. If you cannot check a rule, neither can Claude — vagueness, not attention, is why this rule fails; even the humans disagree on its meaning. Option B raises the priority of a rule that still does not say what to do. Option C moves the same undefined standard into a hook: whether the hook runs a script or a model prompt, 'best practices' gives it nothing concrete to check — the phrasing is the failure, not the enforcement. Option D loads a wall of competing text, and the longer the file, the less reliably Claude follows any single rule. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Write an effective CLAUDE.md

fields.Front: Your CLAUDE.md says 'Don't use default exports.' Claude complies with the ban but improvises the alternative: across 15 recent files, some use named exports, some re-export through index files, and two fall back to CommonJS module.exports, forcing rework. What is the most direct change that makes the rule land consistently? A. Move the rule into its own imported file so it no longer competes with the rules around it. B. Add three few-shot code examples to CLAUDE.md demonstrating named exports in context. C. Escalate the wording to 'YOU MUST not use default exports' to raise its priority. D. Rephrase it as 'Use named exports, not default exports' to name the replacement.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D closes the door the current rule leaves open: a ban without a named replacement invites any alternative, which is exactly the improvisation you are seeing. Naming what to do instead leaves nothing to misinterpret. Option A reorganizes the file but changes nothing about the rule's ambiguity — and imported files are expanded inline anyway. Option B would eventually imply the replacement, but it spends always-loaded context on three code samples to show what one precise sentence states outright; examples earn their place when a transformation is hard to pin down in prose, and this one is not. Option C raises the priority of the prohibition, but Claude is already honoring the prohibition; the failure is in what to do instead, which stronger emphasis on the ban cannot supply. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Write an effective CLAUDE.md • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Over six months, engineers added IMPORTANT or YOU MUST to any rule Claude ignored; 31 of the 40 rules in your project CLAUDE.md now carry that emphasis. This month Claude repeatedly violated the two rules with real consequences: migrations must ship with a rollback plan, and new endpoints must document their auth requirements. How should the team restore the effectiveness of emphasis? A. Move the two critical rules to the top of the file, since rules earlier in the file override later ones. B. Strip the emphasis from routine rules and spend it only on the two or three rules that hurt most when broken. C. Upgrade the two critical rules to all-caps with the warning repeated in consecutive lines. D. Convert all 40 rules into PreToolUse hooks so that none of them depends on Claude's attention.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B applies the principle that emphasis is a budget: IMPORTANT and YOU MUST raise a rule's priority only relative to the quieter rules around it, so when 31 of 40 rules shout, the two that matter get no lift at all. Reserving emphasis for the consequential few restores the contrast that makes it work. Option A relies on an ordering mechanism the file does not have; position is not the lever, relative emphasis is. Option C continues the same inflation arms race that caused the failure. Option D is over-engineered: most of the 40 are soft conventions with no deterministic check a hook could run, and the fix for diluted emphasis is spending it more selectively, not abandoning guidance altogether. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Write an effective CLAUDE.md • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: You are two weeks into a solo refactor on a long-lived branch and want Claude to hold a set of interim architectural decisions in mind every session. The decisions would confuse the other 11 engineers if they applied to their sessions, and they are irrelevant to your other projects. Where should these instructions live? A. In CLAUDE.local.md at the project root, added to .gitignore, where it applies only to you in this repository. B. In the shared project CLAUDE.md, prefixed with a note that only sessions on the refactor branch should apply them. C. In your user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so the decisions follow you without touching the repository. D. In a skill's SKILL.md whose description mentions the refactor, so the decisions load only when they seem relevant.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is exactly what the local location is for: managed-policy, user, project and local instruction files all load together, and CLAUDE.local.md is the one scoped to just you in just this project — you add it to .gitignore so it is never committed. Option B puts personal, interim decisions in the file the whole team shares through version control: once the branch merges, or a teammate checks it out, they load in everyone's sessions, and a disclaimer only hopes each session ignores them. Option C has the wrong scope in the other direction: user-level instructions follow you into every project on your machine. Option D turns standing per-repository context into a conditionally triggered skill; these decisions must be in play every session, not only when a description happens to match. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • How Claude remembers your project — Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — How CLAUDE.md files load (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: To reduce Claude's startup context, a teammate split your 900-line project CLAUDE.md into six files referenced with @.claude/conventions/... imports. The next session's context usage at launch is unchanged, and the teammate files a bug report. What should you tell them? A. Imports load lazily when Claude first needs them, and the launch context meter reports reserved rather than actual usage, so the change did work. B. The @ import syntax requires absolute paths; relative paths such as @.claude/conventions/... silently fall back to inlining every file at launch. C. Imports expand inline at launch, so they organize content without shrinking it; move task-specific material into skills, which load on demand. D. Nest the six files behind a single index file that imports the others, so only the index is read at launch and the rest load when referenced.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C describes the actual mechanism: when Claude launches, imported files are expanded inline right where they are referenced — imports keep a big file tidy, but everything still loads up front, so the meter is telling the truth. Actually shrinking always-loaded context means relocating task-specific material to a surface that loads on demand, such as skills. Options A and B invent behaviors the feature does not have; imports are neither lazy nor path-sensitive in that way. Option D changes nothing, because imports expand recursively — the index pulls in all six files at launch, exactly as the six direct imports did. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • How Claude remembers your project — Import additional files (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features

fields.Front:
Last quarter, 3 of the 20 Claude-assisted refactors your team shipped passed CI only because test assertions had been quietly loosened during the refactor so failing tests would pass. Whether anyone re-checked the diff depended on the individual engineer remembering to ask.

What change most directly closes this gap?

A. A Stop hook that runs the full test suite after every refactor and refuses to let the turn end until every test passes.
B. A verification skill that runs the suite, reads the diff to confirm no test was loosened, and reports pass or fail with evidence.
C. A CLAUDE.md rule, marked IMPORTANT, stating 'Always double-check your work and confirm the tests are still sound before finishing.'
D. Having Claude self-report a confidence score for each refactor so reviewers spend their diff-reading time on the low-confidence ones.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B addresses both failure modes at once. The problem is not tests failing to run — it is tests being weakened so they pass, plus checking that depends on human memory. Claude loads a skill on its own when the skill's description matches the task, so the check no longer waits for someone to ask, and the skill lays out the same written procedure each time; the decisive step is reading the diff to confirm no test was loosened — green alone is not 'done'. Option A guarantees the tests run and pass, but a loosened test passes — the one failure this team actually has is invisible to it. Option C is a vague instruction with no procedure behind it; emphasis raises its priority but still does not say how to check, and it competes for attention with everything else in the file. Option D routes review effort by self-reported confidence, which has no reliable relationship to whether assertions were weakened. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your team's database-migration skill is a single SKILL.md of about 1,100 lines: a 12-step procedure, a full schema-conventions reference, and a 200-line shell script pasted as a code block that Claude is told to copy into a file and run. Every invocation loads all of it into context. How should the skill folder be restructured? A. Split it into three separate skills — procedure, schema reference, and script — each with its own description so every part loads and triggers independently. B. Move the whole skill into the project CLAUDE.md behind an @ import so it loads once at launch instead of on every invocation. C. Condense the procedure, the reference, and the script's steps into summary bullets so the entire SKILL.md fits in far fewer tokens. D. Keep the procedure in a lean SKILL.md, move the schema conventions to a linked reference.md, and ship the script as an executable file in the folder.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D uses what the skill folder is for: the entry file stays short and describes what to do, a reference.md linked from it holds the heavy material and is read only when that depth is needed, and scripts placed in the folder are executed rather than loaded, so the skill carries its own tooling without the script's source entering context. Option A fragments one procedure across three trigger surfaces, and reference text or a script is not itself a task that should fire independently. Option B moves task-specific material into always-loaded memory — the opposite of scoping, and a burden on every session. Option C sacrifices detail the migration genuinely needs when relocating it would have kept both the depth and the lean entry point. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills — Add supporting files (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for skill creators — Structure large skills with progressive disclosure (Agent Skills) • Specification — Progressive disclosure (Agent Skills)

fields.Front: Your pre-release checks skill produces roughly 8,000 tokens of build logs and test output per run. Engineers invoke it several times during long sessions, and after two or three invocations the main conversation fills with stale logs and Claude starts losing track of the feature work. Which frontmatter change fixes this? A. Add context: fork so the skill runs in an isolated subagent context and only a summary comes back. B. Add allowed-tools listing only read-only tools so that each run of the checks generates less output. C. Add argument-hint so engineers can pass a flag that suppresses the build logs and test output. D. Add disable-model-invocation: true so Claude cannot trigger the skill and it runs less often.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A solves the actual problem: with context: fork, the skill executes in a separate subagent context, so its 8,000 tokens of logs land there rather than in the main conversation, only the subagent's summary comes back, and repeated runs stop crowding out the feature work. Option B misreads allowed-tools — the field concerns which tools the skill may use, not how much output a run produces or where that output lands. Option C misreads argument-hint, which is an autocomplete hint showing expected arguments, not a mechanism that changes skill behavior. Option D only stops Claude from triggering the skill automatically; engineers invoke it deliberately, and each manual run would still dump logs into the main context. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills — Run skills in a subagent (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills — Frontmatter reference (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your team's /commit skill walks Claude through staging, writing a message, and committing. The team runs it 30-plus times a day in default (Manual) mode, and every run stops three times for approval of git add, git commit, and git status — a flow the team has fully standardized. What is the most precisely scoped way to remove these prompts? A. Launch the sessions with --permission-mode bypassPermissions so git commands, along with everything else, never prompt. B. Add a Bash(*) allow rule to the project's permission settings so no shell command prompts in any session. C. Add allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *) to the skill's frontmatter. D. State in the body of the skill that git add, git commit, and git status are pre-approved and should run without asking.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C scopes the grant to exactly the standardized flow: allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools for the turn that invokes the skill, so the three prompts disappear only where the team has already decided they add nothing, and the grant clears afterward. Option A removes every permission check in the entire session to fix three prompts — massively over-broad and meant only for isolated environments. Option B permanently pre-approves all shell commands in every context, far beyond the vetted git flow. Option D is prompt-only: permission decisions are made by the permission system, and prose in a skill body cannot grant approval for anything. Currency note (Oct 2026): the exam guide describes allowed-tools as restricting a skill's tool access; current docs say it only pre-approves the listed tools — every other tool stays callable under your normal permission settings — and disallowed-tools is the field that removes tools. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills — Pre-approve tools for a skill (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills — Frontmatter reference (Claude Code docs) • Configure permissions — Permission rule syntax (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your /fix-issue skill expects a GitHub issue number and fails early without one. New teammates invoke it bare from the slash menu about half the time, then sit through a failed run before learning that an argument was required. Which frontmatter addition addresses this? A. context: fork, so that the failed runs at least stay out of the main conversation's context window. B. argument-hint: [issue-number], so autocomplete shows the expected argument as the command is typed. C. allowed-tools: Bash(gh issue list *), so the skill can look up open issues itself without a permission prompt. D. A longer description stating that the skill needs a GitHub issue number before it can do anything.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B fixes the mistake at the moment it happens: argument-hint is the frontmatter surface shown during autocomplete to indicate expected arguments, so a teammate typing /fix-issue sees [issue-number] before submitting a bare invocation. Option A hides the noise of the failure without preventing the failure. Option C pre-approves an issue-listing command, but a bare invocation still gives the skill no way to know which issue the user meant. Option D puts the requirement in the wrong field: the description exists to say what the skill does and when Claude should use it, while argument-hint is the field designed to show expected arguments during autocomplete. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills — Frontmatter reference (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills — Pass arguments to skills (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your project CLAUDE.md contains three things: a 60-line release-checklist procedure used about once a week, naming conventions that apply to every file Claude touches, and a rule that Claude must never disable a failing CI check. Overall adherence has been slipping as the file grows. How should these three items be distributed across instruction surfaces? A. Checklist into a skill; naming conventions stay in CLAUDE.md; the CI rule into a hook that blocks the action. B. Checklist, naming conventions, and the CI rule each into its own skill, so that nothing loads at launch. C. Checklist into an @-imported file; naming conventions and the CI rule stay in CLAUDE.md, marked IMPORTANT. D. Checklist and the CI rule into path-scoped .claude/rules/ files; naming conventions stay in CLAUDE.md.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A follows the three-surface split: conventions that apply all the time belong in CLAUDE.md; procedures tied to a kind of task belong in skills, whose bodies load only when used (only descriptions load until then); and a rule Claude must not be able to skip belongs in a hook, because CLAUDE.md and skills are instructions Claude follows while a hook is enforcement that applies regardless of what Claude decides. Option B evicts always-applicable conventions from the one surface designed for them, leaving routine work unguided, and leaves the hard rule skippable. Option C saves nothing — an imported file is expanded into context at launch, so the weekly procedure still loads every session — and it leaves a must-never rule dependent on emphasis. Option D misapplies path scoping: the checklist is triggered by a kind of task, not a file location, and the CI rule needs enforcement, not conditional loading. fields.Front: Your CLAUDE.md contains the rule IMPORTANT: never run database migrations against the staging database. Across 60 unattended overnight sessions last quarter, Claude ran a staging migration anyway in 3 of them, corrupting shared test data each time. What is the most effective change? A. Move the rule to the top of CLAUDE.md and repeat it in the opening prompt of each unattended overnight session. B. Split CLAUDE.md with @ imports, moving the migration rule into a small, dedicated file of critical rules. C. Switch the overnight sessions to a larger model with --model, keeping the written rule in CLAUDE.md as it is. D. Option D is correct because CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude usually follows, while a hook is deterministic code that runs at a fixed point in the loop: a PreToolUse deny turns "Claude usually listens" into "Claude can't skip it," which is exactly what a 3-in-60 failure rate on unwatched runs demands. Option A raises emphasis, but emphasis is a budget and the rule remains a probabilistic request. Option B reorganizes the file without changing enforcement; imports are expanded inline and everything still loads as guidance. Option C is the bigger-model anti-pattern: the problem is that prompts cannot guarantee behavior, not that the model is too small. fields.Front: You wrote a Claude Code PreToolUse hook to stop Claude from running terraform apply. The script prints blocked: terraform apply is not allowed to stdout and exits with code 1. In all 12 test sessions, the transcript shows a hook error notice for the script, yet Claude still runs terraform apply every time. Why does the command still run? A. PreToolUse hooks only observe tool calls; blocking requires a deny rule in the permission settings instead. B. The message is on stdout; a PreToolUse hook blocks only when its message is printed to stderr instead. C. Exit code 1 is non-blocking; the hook must exit 2, or exit 0 and return JSON with permissionDecision: "deny". D. The hook ran past its timeout; a timed-out PreToolUse command hook does not stop the tool call it guards.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct: exit code 1 feels like an error but does not block on its own — it is treated as a non-blocking error, the transcript shows only a hook error notice, and Claude runs the command anyway. The two blocking paths are exit 2 (with stderr fed back to Claude) or exit 0 with a JSON permissionDecision of deny. Option A is false; PreToolUse is the enforcement primitive and can deny calls before they run, and a deny rule is a separate mechanism, not a prerequisite. Option B misstates the mechanics: blocking is decided by the exit code or a JSON deny, not by which stream carries the message — exit 1 is non-blocking whichever stream the message is on. Option D is contradicted by the stem: a script that prints its message and exits with code 1 finished on its own instead of running past its timeout. A timed-out command hook does not block the call, but that is not what happened here. fields.Front: Your PreToolUse hook redacts sk_live_ secrets from Bash commands by returning updatedInput that contains only the rewritten command field. What is causing the lost fields? A. updatedInput replaces the entire input object, so the hook must echo back every field it is not changing. B. PreToolUse hooks may modify only one allowlisted field per event; changing command clears the rest by design. C. Returning updatedInput without an accompanying permissionDecision: "allow" causes unmodified fields to be dropped. D. The Bash tool re-validates rewritten input and strips any fields the hook did not explicitly approve.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct: updatedInput swaps in a whole new input object rather than patching individual fields, so a hook that returns only command silently discards timeout, run_in_background, and anything else Claude set — the fix is to copy the original input and change just the secret. Option B invents a one-field restriction that does not exist; updatedInput can carry the full object. Option C is wrong because the decision field controls whether the call proceeds, not which fields survive. Option D describes a validation step that does not exist; the fields vanish because the hook's replacement object never included them. fields.Front: You are adding a Claude Code PreToolUse hook as a guardrail for kubectl commands in a shared ops repo. B. allow for dev, deny for prod, and ask for staging so each staging call is handed to the human to approve or reject. C. ask for all three clusters so that no kubectl command ever proceeds without a human review. D. allow for dev and staging, deny for prod, plus a CLAUDE.md note describing when staging commands are risky.

Option A rebuilds ask out of deny plus a prompt instruction, relying on Claude to voluntarily seek approval instead of using the deterministic mechanism. Option C creates prompt fatigue by forcing review of the 100%-safe dev traffic, which erodes attention for the 20% of staging calls that matter. Option D leaves the risky staging window to prompt guidance, which cannot guarantee the roughly one-in-five calls that must be stopped. fields.Front: To keep Claude from writing to infra/prod/, a teammate added a Claude Code PostToolUse hook on the file-edit tools that exits 2 with the message writes to infra/prod are forbidden. Reviewing a week of session logs, you find 4 sessions in which files under infra/prod/ were modified anyway — each modification followed by the hook's message in the transcript. Why is the guardrail failing, and what fixes it? A. Exit code 2 is ignored on file-edit tools, so the hook must return JSON with decision set to block instead. B. The message is on the wrong stream, so it must be written to stdout instead of stderr for the PostToolUse hook to act on it. C. Hooks are unreliable on file-edit tools, so the rule must be stated in CLAUDE.md with IMPORTANT emphasis instead. D. PostToolUse fires after the tool has run, so the check must move to PreToolUse, which denies the write before it happens.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D identifies the root cause: PostToolUse runs after a successful tool call, so by the time the hook fires the file is already modified — exit 2 there can only feed the message back to Claude as context, which is what the transcript shows. Moving the path check to PreToolUse lets the hook deny the edit before it happens. Option A is false: exit 2 is not ignored, it is the blocking exit code on events that support blocking, and a PostToolUse JSON decision of block only adds the reason next to a tool result that already exists, so neither route can undo the write. Option B confuses output channels with blocking behavior: on PostToolUse, exit 2 already shows stderr to Claude, and no choice of stream lets a hook that fires after the write prevent it. Option C retreats to prompt-only enforcement, which is precisely what a hook is supposed to replace for a hard rule, and file-edit tools do fire hooks — the transcript shows the hook's message after each modification. fields.Front: Your release pipeline needs a stage that generates a change summary from the release diff and hands it to the next stage on stdout. Option A depends on an interactive TUI on a runner with no TTY and is brittle by construction. Option C moves the work onto Anthropic's managed infrastructure, so the result never lands on this stage's stdout and the stage gains a polling loop it does not need.
