fields.Front: A nightly headless job asks Claude to list deprecated API calls per file, and a downstream script parses the prose response. The parse step breaks in about 15% of runs because the format drifts — sometimes bullets, sometimes a table, sometimes a paragraph. What is the most reliable fix? A. Add "Respond ONLY with a JSON array and no prose" with --append-system-prompt, and retry the run whenever parsing fails. B. Pass --output-format json and parse the prose in its result field with a more tolerant set of regexes. C. Add a second claude -p call that converts the first run's prose into JSON before the script reads it. D. Pass --output-format json with a --json-schema, and have the script read the structured_output field.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D removes the failure mode instead of coping with it: pairing a JSON schema with JSON output constrains Claude's answer to your schema, and the conforming object lands in structured_output, ready to pull with jq into the next step. Option A is prompt-only compliance — mostly honored, which is exactly how you get a 15% breakage rate — and retries burn pipeline minutes without guaranteeing a parse. Option B wraps the run in JSON metadata, but the answer in result is still free-form prose: the regexes harden the parser against the formats seen so far while leaving it exposed to the next drift. Option C adds a second model invocation to translate output the first invocation could have produced correctly, doubling cost and adding a new place to fail. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Get structured output • CLI reference — CLI flags (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: The same claude -p audit command behaves differently across CI runners and laptops: on some machines it triggers a teammate's ~/.claude PreToolUse hooks, and in one project it connected to the MCP servers in the repo's .mcp.json, adding about 40 seconds of startup. You want every machine to run the identical minimal environment — Claude plus only the tools the script allows explicitly. What change achieves this? A. Add --bare to the command, which skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md. B. Add a setup step that deletes ~/.claude and the repo's .mcp.json from each machine just before the audit command runs. C. Pin the same model version in every environment so that all of the audit runs behave identically. D. Build a container image containing an approved CLAUDE.md and run the audit inside it on every machine.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is the built-in answer: --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md, giving you Claude plus only what the script explicitly allows — the same result on every machine, with faster startup, which is exactly the deterministic behavior CI wants. Option B destroys developers' personal configuration and repo files to simulate what a flag already does, and must be maintained on every machine forever. Option C addresses model behavior, not the real variable — what each machine's environment loads. Option D is over-engineered: standing up container infrastructure to approximate a CLI flag, and whatever configuration ends up in the image is still auto-discovered inside it. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Start faster with bare mode • CLI reference — CLI flags (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your migration automation runs in two stages: at 02:00 a headless run analyzes the codebase and produces a migration plan, and at 04:00 — after a database snapshot completes — a second headless run must execute that plan with full awareness of the analysis, including which files were examined and which approaches were ruled out. How should the second stage obtain that context? A. Include the first run's final plan text in the second run's prompt. B. Combine both stages into one -p invocation that sleeps for two hours between analysis and execution. C. Capture the session_id from the first run's JSON output and start the second stage with --resume. D. Save the first run's full transcript to a file and have the second run load it using a larger context window.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the multi-step automation pattern headless mode supports: the JSON output carries the session ID, and resuming that session at 04:00 restores the full working context — the files examined, the dead ends ruled out, and the plan — so the executor picks up exactly where the analyzer stopped. Option A carries only the plan artifact; the reasoning behind it, which the stem says the executor needs, is lost. Option B holds a runner hostage for two hours and breaks the one-shot semantics of -p, and any failure in the window loses both stages. Option D is the bigger-context anti-pattern: re-ingesting a raw transcript is an expensive, lossy reconstruction of state that --resume restores directly. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Continue conversations • Manage sessions — What a resumed session restores (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: You want a dependency audit to run against your repo every morning at 9am and open a PR when patched versions are available. The team has no CI set up for this repo, nobody wants to maintain a workflow file, and no machine can be left running. Which approach fits these constraints best? A. Create a routine with /schedule so the job runs on Anthropic's managed infrastructure. B. Add a GitHub Actions workflow with a 9am cron trigger that invokes claude -p and opens the PR. C. Run a cron job on a team member's laptop that invokes claude -p at 9am and opens the PR with gh. D. Build a small scheduler service on the Agent SDK, deploy it to your cloud account, and have it run the audit at 9am.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A matches every constraint: a routine bundles a prompt, the repository, and any connectors, and runs on a cron trigger on Anthropic's managed infrastructure — no machine of yours stays on and no workflow file exists to maintain. Recurring, same-prompt work like a morning dependency audit is the canonical routine use case. Option B satisfies the schedule but reintroduces exactly the workflow file the team refuses to own. Option C depends on a laptop being awake and online at 9am every day. Option D is the maximum-effort end of the spectrum — building and hosting a service — for a job whose defining property is that nothing should be built or hosted. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Automate work with routines — Create from the CLI (Claude Code docs) • Automate work with routines — Add a schedule trigger (Claude Code docs) • Run prompts on a schedule — Compare scheduling options (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your nightly Claude Code routine is prompted to "fix one flaky test, push the fix, and carry over notes from the previous night's run." After two weeks you observe: main has zero commits from the routine, its pushes all appear on branches named claude/..., and every night's run re-diagnoses the flakiness from scratch as if the earlier runs never happened. Which explanation matches this behavior? A. GitHub branch protection on main blocks the routine from pushing there, so each night's work lands on separate branches. B. Each run starts from a fresh clone of the default branch and by default pushes its work to a claude/-prefixed branch. C. Routine pushes to protected branches are queued for manual approval and are waiting in the routine dashboard. D. Overnight compaction dropped both the push instruction and the previous night's notes from the routine's context.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B describes how routines are designed to run: every run clones the repository afresh and starts from the default branch — which is why no state or notes persist between nights — and Claude pushes its work to a claude/-prefixed branch by default, which keeps an autonomous run from committing straight to main. Both observed symptoms follow from this one design. Option A names a real control, but it is not what produces these branches: GitHub branch protection governs where a run may push, while the claude/ prefix is simply where a run pushes by default, protected or not, and a protected main would not explain the nightly amnesia. Option C invents an approval queue routines do not have. Option D misattributes a persistent, by-design behavior to compaction, and compaction within one run would not explain fourteen consecutive nights of identical amnesia. Currency note (Oct 2026): earlier descriptions of routines present the claude/ prefix as a restriction you loosen per repository, while current docs describe it as a default that a prompt can override by naming another branch, with GitHub branch protection governing where a run may push. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Automate work with routines — Repositories and branch permissions (Claude Code docs) • Automate work with routines — Create a routine (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front:
After each production deploy completes — at unpredictable times, 3 to 8 times a day — you want a routine to scan the new Sentry errors and file a triage summary. Deploys are driven by an internal release system, not by GitHub.

How should the routine be triggered?

A. An hourly cron schedule, accepting up to an hour of delay after each deploy.
B. A GitHub event trigger on pushes to the release branch, since each deploy corresponds to a release push.
C. A SessionStart hook in the repo that launches the scan whenever a session begins.
D. An HTTP POST from the release system to the routine's API endpoint after each deploy.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D uses the trigger built for this: routines fire on a cron schedule, a GitHub event, or an HTTP POST to their API endpoint, and only the internal release system knows the moment a deploy completes — one POST at that moment gives immediate, exactly-per-deploy runs. Option A turns an event into polling: up to an hour of latency per incident and wasted runs during deploy-free hours. Option B fires at the wrong moment — a push to the release branch is not deploy completion, and the stem says deploys are driven by the internal release system, not GitHub. Option C is a category error: hooks run at fixed points inside a Claude Code session; they are not an external scheduler, and no session is running when the deploy lands. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Automate work with routines — Add an API trigger (Claude Code docs) • Automate work with routines — Configure triggers (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your 8-person team wants every pull request in three repos reviewed by Claude, with findings posted as inline comments on the changed lines and tagged by severity. Nobody wants to build or host anything, and your organization is on an Enterprise plan. What is the most direct path? A. Write a review workflow in each repo using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with a custom review prompt. B. Have an organization Owner enable Code Review in the Claude Code admin settings and select the three repos. C. Ask every engineer to run /code-review locally on each branch before they open a pull request for it. D. Create a routine per repo, triggered on new pull requests, that posts its findings as a PR comment.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is the managed path built for exactly this: an Anthropic-hosted service, enabled once by an organization Owner, that reviews PRs through the Claude GitHub app and posts inline, severity-tagged findings — deduplicated and ranked — with nothing for the team to build or host. Option A wires up custom CI to reproduce what the managed service already does, and now three workflows must be maintained. Option C is manual and unenforced — it depends on each engineer remembering, and a review run before the PR exists leaves its findings in that engineer's terminal rather than on the changed lines of the PR. Option D rebuilds review on routine infrastructure without the managed service's review pipeline, and a single rolled-up comment is not inline findings on changed lines. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Code Review — Set up Code Review (Claude Code docs) • Code Review — How reviews work (Claude Code docs) • Claude Code GitHub Actions

fields.Front: Beyond review comments, your team wants this behavior: when a developer comments @claude implement the spec in the linked issue on a pull request, Claude should push commits to that PR's branch and post a comment describing what it did. Claude Code's managed Code Review is already enabled on the repo. What should you add? A. Nothing new — configure managed Code Review's @claude review trigger to also apply the changes it suggests. B. A routine with a GitHub trigger on pull_request.opened that implements the linked spec on the PR's branch. C. A workflow using anthropics/claude-code-action@v1, set up with /install-github-app, that answers @claude mentions. D. A Stop hook in .claude/settings.json that implements the linked spec whenever a review session finishes its turn.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is the do-it-yourself path for jobs that go beyond review: the GitHub Action runs the agent on PR and issue comments, so an @claude mention (the default trigger_phrase) kicks off a run that pushes commits and posts comments — exactly the requested behavior — and /install-github-app handles app installation and the API key secret. Option A misreads the managed service's boundaries: it posts findings only, never applies changes, and never approves or blocks. Option B uses a real routine trigger but answers the wrong event: the GitHub events a routine can subscribe to are pull request and release events, such as pull_request.opened, and the filters match PR fields like author, title, body, branches and labels, not comment text, so a routine cannot be started by an @claude comment — and a routine run starts from the default branch and pushes to a claude/-prefixed branch by default, not the PR's own branch. Option D is a category error: hooks fire at lifecycle points inside a Claude Code session, not in response to GitHub comment events. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Interactive and automation modes • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Quick setup • Code Review — How reviews work (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your scheduled repository-report workflow uses anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with a plain-text prompt. Last month one run looped for 47 turns before the job was killed at its 6-hour timeout, and two runs produced no report because every call to the GitHub tools Claude needs for reading commits and issues was denied. The report only needs to read commits and issues and write a summary to the run log. Which TWO configuration changes best fix these failures? (Select TWO.) A. Raise the workflow's timeout-minutes limit beyond the six hours that killed the looping run. B. Name the GitHub read tools the report needs in --allowedTools, passed through claude_args. C. Pass --dangerously-skip-permissions through claude_args alongside the plain-text prompt. D. Cap the agent loop by passing a turn limit with --max-turns through claude_args.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B and D. Option B fixes the empty reports at the root: with a plain-text prompt the action gives Claude no shell or GitHub API access until the workflow grants the tools the prompt needs, and --allowedTools in claude_args is where that grant goes — naming only the read tools keeps the job scoped to what a report requires. Option D fixes the runaway: a --max-turns cap in claude_args puts a hard ceiling on the agent loop, ending a 47-turn spiral deterministically. Option A extends the runaway rather than curing it — a looping run just consumes more billable minutes before it is killed. Option C trades the denials for unbounded privilege: a read-only report should be scoped to read-only tools, and skipping every permission check does nothing about looping. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Run on a schedule • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Manage costs • Claude Code GitHub Actions — Pass CLI arguments

fields.Front: You wired your own PR-review workflow with claude-code-action@v1; it runs on every push and gives Claude only the current diff. Active PRs average 6 pushes, and by merge time each carries roughly 40 review comments — mostly the same findings re-posted by later runs, plus dozens of style nits. Reviewers have started ignoring the bot, but the team, which is on a Team plan, wants every push to keep being reviewed. What is the most effective change? A. Replace the workflow with managed Code Review, which deduplicates and ranks findings and resolves fixed threads. B. Add "do not repeat findings already posted by earlier runs, and skip style nits" to the workflow's review prompt. C. Trigger the review only when the PR is opened or marked ready for review, so each PR is commented on exactly once. D. Cap the workflow at five comments per run, ordered by the model's own severity rating, so the total volume stays manageable.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A fixes both symptoms with the service designed for them: the managed review pipeline deduplicates and ranks findings by severity and, when it reviews every push, resolves a thread once the flagged issue is fixed, so reviewers read a short list of real issues rather than a wall of repeats and nits. Option B is an instruction this workflow gives the model no way to follow — each run is a fresh instance that sees only the current diff, so it has no record of earlier findings to check against; the instruction works only when prior findings are passed into the run's context. Option C removes duplication by abandoning the stated requirement that every push stays reviewed. Option D is an arbitrary cap: five comments per run still repeat the same findings across the 6 runs, and a per-run self-rating is no substitute for deduplication across runs. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Code Review — How reviews work (Claude Code docs) • Code Review — Set up Code Review (Claude Code docs) • Claude Code GitHub Actions

fields.Front:
Your automation pipeline has one Claude instance implement a change from an issue, then a separate fresh instance review the resulting PR. A teammate proposes feeding the implementer's session transcript into the review run "so the reviewer understands the intent and stops flagging things the implementer already considered."

How should you respond to the proposal?

A. Accept it, but pass a condensed summary of the transcript instead of the full text, because that saves tokens.
B. Reject it, because implementation transcripts are too large to fit in the review run's context window.
C. Accept it, because a reviewer that knows the intent will produce fewer false-positive findings.
D. Reject it, because a reviewer unaware of how the code was built catches what the implementer talked itself past.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D preserves the property that makes the second instance valuable: fresh context. A cold reviewer judges the code on its own merits, so the rationalizations the implementer "already considered" get re-tested instead of inherited — that is precisely how it catches what the original run talked itself past. Option A imports the implementer's framing in condensed form, recreating the same blind spots at lower token cost. Option B rejects for the wrong reason; the principle is independence, not context size, and a summary would fit anyway. Option C is the trap in the proposal itself: the findings suppressed as "already considered" are exactly the ones an independent review exists to surface. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions

fields.Front: An unattended overnight Claude Code run reports: "Refactored the payment retry logic in src/billing/retry.ts; all 214 tests pass." CI independently ran the full suite and is green. You have 15 minutes before standup to decide whether this is ready for a pull request. Where should you spend those 15 minutes first? A. The run's summary, cross-checking each file and test count it names against the repository state. B. The session transcript, reopened with claude --resume and read from the beginning of the run, step by step. C. The diff itself, via /code-review and then git diff, checking for changes outside the file the run names. D. A fresh claude -p session's opinion on whether the summary and the CI result together sound complete and plausible.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C follows the core rule for unsupervised work: start from the diff, not the summary. The trap is a tidy write-up that reads fine while the diff quietly touched files you did not expect; /code-review flags issues and your own pass over git diff — the named file first, then anything outside it — is what exposes scope surprises, the one risk the green test suite does not cover. Option A is bounded by what the summary chooses to mention, which is exactly the untrusted artifact. Option B narrates intent step by step and will not fit a 15-minute window; effects live in the diff. Option D asks a model to review prose about the code rather than the code, so an omission in the summary survives the check. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Code Review — Review a diff locally (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Avoid common failure patterns

fields.Front:
After a 3-hour unsupervised Claude Code run produced a large diff, you asked the same session to "critically review your own work." It reported zero issues. A human skim later found a subtle concurrency bug in code the session had rewritten twice during the run.

Which review setup would most likely have caught the bug?

A. Asking the original session to review again with stronger wording, such as "be far more critical on this pass."
B. Having the original session rate its confidence per file, then reviewing only the files rated below 80%.
C. Re-running the entire task in a second session and diffing the two resulting implementations.
D. Having a fresh session or subagent review the diff with no memory of how the code was built.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is the cold second opinion: a reviewer with no memory of the run has no stake in the approach, so the reasoning that talked the original session past the concurrency bug — twice — carries no weight with it, and the code is judged on what it actually does. Option A adds emphasis but keeps the same stakeholder; the blind spot that produced the bug also hides it from self-review. Option B routes attention by self-reported confidence, an unreliable signal — the session was confident enough to rewrite that code twice and report zero issues. Option C is over-engineered: two divergent implementations produce a wall of incidental differences that localizes nothing, at double the cost of simply reviewing the diff that exists. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions

fields.Front: A nightly headless job runs claude -p across 30 repos to apply a dependency bump, and you have about 20 minutes each morning to triage. Today you skim all 30 prose outputs, which consumes the whole window and has still missed 2 failed runs this month. What triage process should replace this? A. Check each run's exit code and JSON result first, then spend the time on failures and a sample of passing diffs. B. Pipe the 30 outputs into one Claude session and read its combined summary of what succeeded and what failed. C. Have each run append a self-assessed confidence percentage and review the runs that score below the 80% mark. D. Replace the morning triage with investigating whichever repos have a CI failure reported later in the day.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A applies the rule for headless work — verify runs by their JSON result and exit code. Those signals are machine-checkable, so the 2 failures this month would surface in seconds instead of being lost in prose, and the reclaimed time goes where judgment matters: the failing runs plus a rotating sample of passing diffs, which is how trust in the other 28 is earned rather than assumed. Option B trades 30 summaries for a summary of summaries — the same trust-the-prose failure mode, aggregated. Option C routes attention by self-reported confidence, which is not a reliable escalation signal. Option D is purely reactive: regressions ship and CI becomes your users' first reviewer. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Basic usage • Best practices for Claude Code — Fan out across files

fields.Front:
Your team is scaling unattended auto-mode runs from 5 to 40 per week. Verification today is: read Claude's summary, and trust that auto mode's classifier reviewed each action. Two regressions shipped last month from runs whose summaries claimed "all tests pass."

Which TWO changes would give these runs real verification? (Select TWO.)

A. Wire the test suite as a Stop hook that refuses to end the turn on failure, so tests gate every session.
B. Keep relying on the auto-mode classifier but configure it more strictly, since it already reviews actions.
C. Require each run's summary to quote the test command and its full output verbatim as proof of the result.
D. Add a fresh-context review of each run's diff, by a new session or subagent, before anything merges.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A and D. Option A turns tests from a claim into a gate: the Stop hook runs the suite itself and refuses to end the turn on failure, so "all tests pass" can no longer be asserted without being true, and the exit-2 feedback lets Claude fix failures unprompted — closing the exact hole behind last month's regressions. Option D adds the cold second opinion: a fresh-context reviewer of the diff has no stake in the approach and catches what the run talked itself past, which matters most when nobody watched the run. Option B misunderstands the classifier: it guards dangerous actions and never judges correctness, so no strictness setting makes it catch broken code. Option C is still self-reported — a summary is authored by the same run being verified, and quoted output can be stale or wrong with nobody checking it. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Give Claude a way to verify its work • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Choose a permission mode — Eliminate permission prompts with auto mode (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: A teammate installed a community-marketplace plugin at project scope for its SQL-formatting skill. A week later you notice that every Claude Code session in that project makes an outbound network request each time Claude ends its turn. Nothing in your own .claude configuration references that endpoint. What explains the requests, and what should have happened before installing? A. Claude Code telemetry makes the calls, and a plugin listed in the community marketplace is vetted, so it is not the source. B. Plugins run in a sandbox without network access, so an MCP server configured in the project is making the calls. C. The plugin bundled a Stop hook that fires each turn, so its hooks and MCP servers needed review before installing. D. Installing a plugin for one skill adds just that skill, so someone else added the hook to the project separately.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C matches both the symptom and the remedy: a plugin is one installable unit, so installing it for a skill also installs its hooks — a bundled Stop hook fires on every turn, stacking alongside your own hooks rather than appearing in your configuration — and a plugin runs code on your machine with your privileges, which is why reading its components before install is the rule. Option A treats a marketplace listing as a guarantee, but a marketplace's name tells you who publishes the catalog, not what each plugin in it does, so a listed plugin can still be the source; nothing in the scenario points to telemetry, while a request at the end of every turn is what a Stop hook produces. Option B invents a network sandbox plugins do not have: a plugin's hooks run as shell commands with your full user permissions. Option D gets the bundling model backwards: you get every component the plugin ships, whether you wanted it or not. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Plugin security and trust — Understand what a plugin can do (Claude Code docs) • Plugin security and trust — Review a plugin before you install (Claude Code docs) • Install and manage plugins — Choose an install scope (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your platform team's .claude setup — 6 skills, 2 subagents, a hooks file, and an MCP config — works well. Thirty engineers across 12 repos currently copy the folder around by hand; after the latest update, 11 of them were found still running a version with a broken hook that had been fixed three weeks earlier. What distribution approach fixes this? A. Commit the .claude folder to a template repository that engineers copy when creating new projects. B. Package the setup as a plugin in a private marketplace so everyone installs and updates from one place. C. Merge the six skills' contents into a shared CLAUDE.md that is redistributed whenever it changes. D. Have each engineer maintain a personal fork of the folder and cherry-pick fixes as they land.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is what plugins are for: the existing skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP config move into one installable unit without being rewritten, and a private marketplace added once (/plugin marketplace add) lets every engineer install it and keep receiving updates from a catalog you control, so the 11 stale copies become a plugin update — automatic where auto-update is turned on — instead of a hunt across laptops. Option A helps only at project creation; the 12 existing repos keep drifting exactly as they do today. Option C moves task-scoped procedures onto the always-loaded guidance surface — every line now competes for attention in every session — and the distribution problem remains manual. Option D makes drift the design: 30 forks cherry-picking independently is how the broken-hook situation happened. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Create a marketplace (Claude Code docs) • Create a Claude Code plugin — Convert an existing .claude/ setup • Install and manage plugins — Add a private marketplace (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your team uses Claude Code on a repository whose project CLAUDE.md says 'Prefer named exports.' Across roughly 200 sessions last month, Claude wrote a default export twice; each one was caught in code review and fixed in under a minute, and neither reached production. Files under app/pages/ have to use default exports because the framework's router requires them, so some default exports are correct. A teammate proposes a hook that blocks any file edit containing export default. What is the right response to the proposal? A. Adopt the proposal as a PreToolUse hook that denies each file edit whose new content contains export default. B. Keep the rule in the project CLAUDE.md, reword it to state the app/pages/ exception, and leave the rare miss to code review. C. Rewrite the rule in the project CLAUDE.md as 'YOU MUST NEVER use default exports' and repeat it at the top and at the bottom of the file. D. Add a Stop hook that keeps Claude from ending its turn while the diff for the session contains a default export.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. A hook is the tool for a rule that has to hold every time; CLAUDE.md is the place for conventions Claude should follow. This rule is a style preference: a miss costs one review comment, and the app/pages/ files show that it should not hold every time. Guidance that names the exception fits the rule, and the rare miss stays cheap. Option A turns a preference into a hard block, and that block would also stop the default exports the router requires. Option C only raises the volume: the rule remains a request, and as reworded it is wrong for page files. Option D has the same defect as A at a later point, because it would refuse to end turns that correctly edited a page file, and a Stop gate is far heavier machinery than a two-in-200 style slip warrants. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • Best practices for Claude Code — Set up hooks • How Claude remembers your project — CLAUDE.md vs auto memory (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: To keep Terraform files under infra/ consistently formatted, a teammate added a Claude Code PreToolUse hook on the file-edit tools that runs terraform fmt on the file named in the tool input and exits 0. Reviewing a week of session logs, you find 4 sessions in which Claude's edits to existing files under infra/ were committed unformatted, although the logs show that the hook ran before each of those edits and that the formatter exited without error. Why is the formatting step failing, and what fixes it? A. PreToolUse runs before the edit is applied, so the formatter sees the old contents; move the command to a PostToolUse hook on the same tools. B. A hook that exits 0 is treated as having changed nothing, so its formatting is discarded; have the hook exit 2 after it runs the formatter. C. The file-edit tools write through a path that skips hooks, so the formatter is not reached; state the formatting rule in CLAUDE.md with emphasis. D. A PreToolUse hook has to return a decision to take effect, so the run is ignored; return permissionDecision: "deny" until the file is formatted.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A identifies the root cause. A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool call executes, so terraform fmt formats the file as it was, and the edit then writes new, unformatted content. A step that depends on the result of an edit belongs on PostToolUse, which runs immediately after a tool completes successfully; a PostToolUse hook matched to the file-edit tools is the documented way to format the files Claude edits. Option B is wrong because exit 0 means the hook succeeded and the formatter's changes on disk stand, while exit 2 on PreToolUse would block the edit. Option C contradicts the logs, which show the hook firing on these tools, and it replaces a step that should run on each edit with an instruction. Option D is wrong because a command hook runs whether or not it returns a decision, and a deny would block the edits and leave formatting to Claude. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.4 References: • Automate actions with hooks — Auto-format code after edits (Claude Code docs) • Hooks reference — PostToolUse (Claude Code docs) • Hooks reference — PreToolUse (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your team is building a billing-support agent for an electricity utility with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent acts through tools that include apply_credit and schedule_disconnection. Its system prompt holds four rules: (1) do not apply an account credit above $200 without supervisor approval; (2) mention paperless billing when a customer raises a late paper bill; (3) do not schedule a disconnection for an account that carries a medical-hold flag; (4) address customers by the preferred name on file. In last month's 1,400 conversations the agent applied a credit above $200 three times and scheduled one disconnection on a flagged account. How should the four rules be implemented? A. Enforce rules 1 and 3 in hooks that intercept the credit and disconnection tool calls, and keep rules 2 and 4 in the system prompt. B. Enforce rules 2 and 4 in hooks, and keep rules 1 and 3 in the system prompt with few-shot examples that show the correct handling. C. Move the four rules out of the system prompt, and enforce each of them in a hook that intercepts the agent's outgoing tool calls. D. Keep the four rules in the system prompt, and restate rules 1 and 3 in capital letters at both the start and the end of the system prompt.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Rules 1 and 3 are business rules with financial and safety consequences, and three over-limit credits and one wrongful disconnection show that prompt instructions leave a non-zero failure rate. A hook that intercepts the outgoing apply_credit and schedule_disconnection calls decides in code, so it blocks a violating call each time, and the reason it returns tells the agent to route the case to a supervisor. Rules 2 and 4 are preferences about conversation; an occasional miss costs little, and a prompt handles them well. Option B splits the rules the wrong way round: the two that need a guarantee stay as instructions, where few-shot examples lower the failure rate without removing it, and hooks are spent on a suggestion and a form of address, which are not tool calls for a hook to intercept. Option C over-builds for the same reason, and taking rules 2 and 4 out of the prompt removes guidance the model needs. Option D leaves rules 1 and 3 as instructions; emphasis lowers the failure rate without removing it, which is not enough where a miss cuts off power to a protected customer. Domain 1 (Agentic Architecture & Orchestration) · Task 1.5 References: • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — Add context and block a tool • Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks — How hooks work • Hooks reference — PreToolUse decision control (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: You and two other engineers are two weeks into a refactor of the services/ledger/ directory in a monorepo, and you want Claude to hold a set of interim architectural decisions in mind whenever one of the three of you works on that code. The decisions would confuse the other 9 engineers, who work elsewhere in the repository, if they loaded in their sessions, and they are irrelevant to your other projects. The whole team starts Claude Code from the repository root. Where should these instructions live? A. In CLAUDE.local.md at the repository root, added to .gitignore and maintained on your own machine. B. In a CLAUDE.md file inside services/ledger/, committed to the repository alongside the code that is being refactored. C. In the project CLAUDE.md at the repository root, under a heading that marks them as applying to work on the ledger. D. In the user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md of each of the three engineers, copied by hand between their machines.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. The decisions belong to one directory and to the people who work in it, which is what a directory-level CLAUDE.md provides: it is committed, so the three of you share it through version control, and a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory is not loaded at launch but is included when Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory. Sessions that do not touch that directory do not load it. Option A is the personal, per-project file; it stays on your machine, so your two colleagues would not receive the decisions. Option C loads at launch in the sessions of the 12 engineers and relies on each session to disregard a section, which is the confusion you set out to avoid. Option D is personal configuration that is not shared through version control, follows each engineer into unrelated projects, and drifts as soon as one copy changes. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • How Claude remembers your project — How CLAUDE.md files load (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — Choose where to put CLAUDE.md files (Claude Code docs) • Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase — Layer CLAUDE.md files by directory

fields.Front: Your team's /handoff skill tells Claude to write a short handoff note covering the decisions made and the open questions raised so far in the current session; a typical note is about 300 tokens, and engineers run the skill at the end of long working sessions. To keep skill output out of the main conversation, a teammate added context: fork to the skill's frontmatter. Since that change, each note has been generic: it describes the repository and mentions none of the decisions made in the session. Which frontmatter change fixes this? A. Add agent: Explore so that the forked subagent searches the session for the decisions before it writes the note. B. Add background: false so that the forked subagent finishes reading the conversation before it writes the note. C. Add disable-model-invocation: true so that the skill runs when an engineer has finished making decisions. D. Remove context: fork so that the skill runs inline in the main conversation, where the decisions are in context.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. With context: fork, Claude Code starts a new subagent and gives it the skill content as its prompt; that subagent does not see the conversation history. A note about this session's decisions therefore has nothing to draw on, which explains the generic output. Forking suits self-contained tasks with bulky output, and this skill is the opposite case: its output is small and its input is the conversation, so it should run inline. Option A changes the subagent type, but no subagent type started this way receives the history. Option B makes the session wait for the forked subagent's result; it does not change what that subagent sees. Option C controls who starts the skill, not the context it runs in, so a manually started fork would be just as blind to the session. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude with skills — Run skills in a subagent (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills — Frontmatter reference (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: To slim down your project CLAUDE.md, a teammate moved three things out of it and into one skill named team-standards: the naming conventions that apply to every file Claude touches, the build and test commands, and a 60-line release-checklist procedure used about once a week. Since the move, Claude follows the checklist correctly when someone asks for a release, but in everyday sessions it often runs the wrong test command and ignores the naming conventions. How should these three items be placed? A. Keep the three items in the skill, and rewrite its description to state that it applies to each coding task. B. Return the release checklist to CLAUDE.md, and keep the naming conventions and the commands in the skill. C. Return the naming conventions and the commands to CLAUDE.md, and keep the release checklist in a skill. D. Move the three items into a PreToolUse hook that adds them to context before each file edit.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. CLAUDE.md is loaded in each session, so it is the place for what Claude should always know: coding conventions and build and test commands. A skill is loaded on demand, when someone invokes it or Claude judges it relevant, which suits a weekly release procedure and explains why the checklist works while the everyday standards go missing. Option A keeps universal standards behind a loading decision that Claude makes per task; a broader description raises the odds without making the standards always present, and it would pull a 60-line checklist into routine work. Option B splits the items the wrong way round: the checklist, needed about once a week, would be loaded in each session, while the conventions and commands that each session needs would still wait on the skill being loaded. Option D uses an enforcement mechanism to deliver guidance and would add the checklist to context before each edit. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.2 References: • Extend Claude Code — Compare similar features • How Claude remembers your project — When to add to CLAUDE.md (Claude Code docs) • Extend Claude with skills — Control who invokes a skill (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your payments conventions apply only to code under packages/payments/, one of 14 packages in a monorepo. The payments team owns that directory, revises the conventions every few weeks, and wants each revision to ship in the same pull request as the code it describes. The repository's root .claude/ directory belongs to the platform team, and a change there needs that team's review. A teammate proposes delivering the conventions as a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/. What is the better mechanism? A. The proposed .claude/rules/payments.md with paths: ["packages/payments/**"] frontmatter, kept under the root .claude/ directory. B. A "Payments" section in the root CLAUDE.md, loaded at launch in the sessions of the engineers who work on the 14 packages. C. A CLAUDE.md file inside packages/payments/, maintained by the payments team and versioned with the package's code. D. A payments-conventions skill under .claude/skills/, loaded when Claude judges that a task concerns payments.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. Per-directory CLAUDE.md files and path-scoped rules both target part of the tree; they differ in where the file lives. The docs recommend a CLAUDE.md inside the directory when directory owners maintain their own conventions and want instructions versioned with the code, and a central rule when one rule covers many scattered paths. Here the conventions belong to one directory and one owning team, so a CLAUDE.md in packages/payments/ ships in the team's own pull requests and loads when Claude works there. Option A would deliver the same content, but it places the file where each revision waits on the platform team, and nothing here is scattered. Option B puts payments conventions into the launch context of sessions on the other 13 packages. Option D makes conventions that should apply whenever payments code is edited depend on Claude choosing to load a skill. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.3 References: • Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase — Choose between per-directory CLAUDE.md and path-scoped rules • Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase — Layer CLAUDE.md files by directory • How Claude remembers your project — How CLAUDE.md files load (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front:
Your team uses Claude Code mostly for small maintenance fixes: a typo in a log message, a missing null check that a stack trace points to, a variable renamed inside one function. A team rule requires each session to start in plan mode, so engineers read and approve a plan before a fix is made. The plans are approved without edits in nearly every case, and the step adds about ten minutes to changes that the engineer could have described in one sentence.

What working habit would most reduce this overhead?

A. Have Claude make clearly scoped fixes like these directly, and reserve plan mode for multi-file or uncertain changes.
B. Keep plan mode for each fix, and ask Claude to limit its plan to three bullet points that the engineer approves.
C. Keep plan mode for each fix, and have the Explore subagent research the plan and return a summary to the session.
D. Collect a day's fixes into one session, and have Claude write one plan for the batch before it starts editing.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. Plan mode pays for itself when the approach is uncertain, when a change spans multiple files, or when the code is unfamiliar; it adds overhead when the scope is clear and the fix is small. These fixes sit in one function, are pinned down by a stack trace or a one-sentence description, and their plans are approved unchanged, so the plan contributes nothing but delay. Direct execution suits them, and plan mode stays available for larger work. Option B shortens each plan but keeps a review step that has no decision to inform. Option C adds a subagent to research that these fixes do not need; the Explore subagent earns its place when discovery is verbose. Option D merges unrelated fixes into one session and one larger plan, which fills the context with unrelated work and leaves each fix waiting on a plan. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code • Choose a permission mode — Analyze before you edit with plan mode (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: You are about to add live order-status updates to a UI prototype with Claude Code. Claude could build the feature with polling, with server-sent events or with WebSockets; each choice places different infrastructure requirements on the backend team, from load-balancer settings to connection limits, and you have not decided between them. Your usual way of working on this prototype is to let Claude edit freely and to review each change by refreshing the browser. Which mode should the session start in for this task? A. acceptEdits mode, in which Claude applies file edits without asking and you judge each approach by trying it in the browser. B. plan mode, in which Claude researches the code and proposes an approach for you to approve before changes are made. C. auto mode, in which Claude works without routine prompts while a classifier model reviews its actions before they run. D. default (Manual) mode, in which Claude asks before each file edit and you approve or decline the edits one at a time.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Plan mode is meant for tasks with multiple valid approaches and architectural consequences: Claude researches and proposes changes without making them, and you approve a plan before implementation starts. Here three designs are possible, each commits the backend team to different infrastructure, and the choice has not been made, so the decision should be settled before code exists. Option A suits the usual edit-and-refresh loop on this prototype, but it has Claude start building one design, and the browser shows how a page behaves, not what the backend has to run. Option C removes prompts for a direction that has not been chosen; its classifier screens risky actions, not design choices. Option D lets you decline edits one at a time, yet Claude is implementing a design it picked, and you would be reviewing code line by line without a comparison of the alternatives. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.4 References: • Choose a permission mode — Analyze before you edit with plan mode (Claude Code docs) • Choose a permission mode — Available modes (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Explore first, then plan, then code

fields.Front: A CI job runs claude -p to generate unit tests for the files changed in each pull request. The repository's project CLAUDE.md documents the team's testing standards and its shared fixtures. Two weeks ago a teammate added --bare to the command to shorten startup. From that point the generated tests have built their own mock data and ignored the shared fixtures, and reviewers reject most of them. The CI runners hold no user-level configuration, and the repository defines no hooks or MCP servers. What change restores the quality of the generated tests? A. Add --output-format json with a --json-schema that requires a fixtures_used field in each result. B. Copy the project CLAUDE.md to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on each CI runner as user-level instructions. C. Run the job twice for each pull request, and keep only the tests that appear in both of the runs. D. Remove --bare from the command, and let the run load the project CLAUDE.md as it used to.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. CLAUDE.md is how a CI-invoked run receives project context such as testing standards and available fixtures, and --bare skips auto-discovery of CLAUDE.md along with hooks, skills and MCP servers. The standards are documented; the flag keeps them out of the run. Nothing else on these runners needs excluding, so removing the flag restores the context at no cost. Option A constrains the shape of the output, and a schema field does not tell Claude which fixtures exist or what the standards say. Option B fails because the flag stays on the command, and bare mode skips CLAUDE.md discovery at user level as well as project level. Option C compares two runs that both lack the standards, so agreement between them says nothing about fixture use. Currency note (Oct 2026): current docs recommend --bare for scripted runs and say it will become the default for -p; a bare job has to be handed its standards explicitly, for example with --append-system-prompt-file. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Start faster with bare mode • CLI reference — CLI flags (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — Set up a project CLAUDE.md (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your migration automation runs in two stages on one CI runner: at 02:00 a headless run writes the migration scripts from a list of requirements, and at 04:00 — after a database snapshot completes — a second headless run must check those scripts for defects before a human approves them. The 04:00 check exists to catch mistakes that the 02:00 run made, such as a wrong assumption about a column that it went on to build into several scripts. The first run's session ID and transcript are both available to the second stage. How should the second stage be set up? A. Start a new claude -p run, and give it the migration scripts and the list of requirements as its input. B. Capture the session_id from the first run's JSON output, and start the second run with --resume and that ID. C. Start a new claude -p run, and give it the scripts together with the first run's transcript file as its input. D. Add a closing review instruction to the first claude -p run's prompt, and move that single run to 04:00.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct. A session that generated code is less effective at reviewing it, because it retains the reasoning that produced the code and is unlikely to question its own decisions; an independent instance that sees only the scripts and the requirements judges them on their merits. The second stage here is a review, so it should start fresh. Option B restores the first run's full context, which is the right pattern when a later stage has to carry the earlier work forward, but it hands the reviewer the same wrong assumption the check is meant to catch. Option C starts a new session and then imports the first run's reasoning through its transcript, which recreates the blind spot. Option D is self-review inside the generating session, where the reasoning behind each script is in context and each mistake has already been accepted once. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions • Run Claude Code programmatically — Continue conversations

fields.Front: Your pull-request pipeline has a stage that pipes each PR diff to Claude Code for review on an ephemeral CI runner with no TTY. The stage after it is a script that posts every finding as an inline comment through the code host's API, and for each finding it needs the file path, the line number, a severity and the comment text as separate fields. Over the past week the script failed on several PRs because the review text it received varied in layout between runs, with findings sometimes grouped under headings or preceded by introductory prose. How should the review stage invoke Claude Code? A. Run claude -p with the diff on stdin, and have the prompt require one path:line:severity line per finding. B. Run claude -p with --output-format stream-json, and have the script collect findings from the streamed events. C. Run claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema, and have the script read fields from structured_output. D. Run claude in acceptEdits mode with the diff as its opening prompt, and have the script read the terminal output.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The consumer is a script that needs path, line, severity and text as separate fields, and --output-format json with --json-schema returns output validated against a schema you define, delivered in the structured_output field alongside run metadata, so the script parses fields rather than prose. Option A is the right design when the stage after it only passes text along, since -p reads stdin and writes stdout like any shell tool, but a layout requested in the prompt is not validated and the review text can keep varying. Option B emits newline-delimited events meant for real-time streaming, and the review text carried inside those events is no more structured than plain output. Option D depends on an interactive terminal session that a runner with no TTY cannot provide, and acceptEdits governs which actions run without approval, not the shape of the output. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.6 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Get structured output • Run Claude Code programmatically — Pipe data through Claude • CLI reference — CLI flags (Claude Code docs)

fields.Front: Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to about 700 lines over two years. One line reads 'Use named exports, not default exports.' Across 15 recent files Claude followed that rule in nine and wrote default exports in six, and several other rules in the file are being skipped in the same uneven way. A read-through finds long passages describing standard TypeScript practice that Claude follows without being told, a listing of the directory layout, and setup steps for a build tool the team retired last year. Which change is most likely to make these rules land consistently? A. Rephrase the rule to spell out the replacement, such as 'Export each symbol by name from the module that defines it.' B. Split the file into topic files by subject, and reference each of them from CLAUDE.md with an @path import. C. Cut the file down by removing what Claude already does unprompted, the layout listing and the retired tool's steps. D. Mark the export rule and each of the other skipped rules with IMPORTANT, and move them to the top of the file.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: C. Option C is correct. The rule already says what to do, and it is followed in some files and skipped in others along with several unrelated rules, which points at the file and not at the wording: a CLAUDE.md far past the recommended length consumes context and lowers adherence, so rules get lost among content that earns no place. Removing what Claude does correctly without instruction, what it can derive from the codebase and what is obsolete lets the remaining rules register. Option A is the right repair when a rule bans something without naming an alternative, but this rule names one. Option B reorganizes the same 700 lines, because imported files are loaded at launch alongside the file that references them. Option D spends emphasis on a lengthening list of rules and reorders them, while the hundreds of lines that bury them stay loaded. Domain 3 (Claude Code Configuration & Workflows) · Task 3.1 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Write an effective CLAUDE.md • How Claude remembers your project — Write effective instructions (Claude Code docs) • How Claude remembers your project — My CLAUDE.md is too large (Claude Code docs) • Best practices for Claude Code — Avoid common failure patterns

fields.Front: Four hours into a Claude Code session you have traced a legacy billing retry flow: eleven classes are involved, and three suspected causes of a duplicate-charge bug have been ruled out with evidence. The context window is nearly full, and none of the findings has been recorded outside the conversation. You will be away from tomorrow, and a teammate will take over the investigation on their own laptop, working in their own clone of the repository. What should you do before you stop so that the investigation carries on without the findings being lost? A. Run /compact with instructions to keep the class map and ruled-out causes, and have the teammate resume work from the compacted summary. B. Leave the session open, and have the teammate run claude --continue in their own clone to load the conversation. C. End the session with /exit, and have the teammate's fresh session trace the retry flow from the source code. D. Have Claude write the class map and ruled-out causes to docs/retry-notes.md, commit and push it, and have the teammate's session read it.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. The investigation carries on in a different session on another machine, so the findings have to cross a context boundary, and a file in the repository is something a new session can read: the class map and the evidence for each ruled-out cause arrive intact. Option A is the right move for freeing context when the same session keeps working, but the summary it produces stays inside that session on your laptop. Option B loads the most recent conversation in the current directory of the machine it runs on, and transcripts are stored locally, so the teammate's clone has nothing of yours to load. Option C discards what the session learned and pays for the four hours twice, with the risk that a cause already eliminated gets investigated a second time. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.4 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Manage context aggressively • Manage sessions — Where transcripts are stored (Claude Code docs) • CLI reference — CLI flags (Claude Code docs) • Prompting best practices — Workflows across multiple context windows

fields.Front: A nightly headless job runs claude -p across 30 repositories to apply dependency bumps. A wrapper script checks each run's exit code and JSON result and alerts you to failures, and each morning you review the failures plus three passing diffs picked at random. The dashboard reports 29 or 30 passing runs on a typical night. Twice this month a run that exited 0 had pinned an incompatible version, which was found only after deployment, and both cases were among the four Python repositories; the other 26 repositories are TypeScript. Which change to the review process best addresses this? A. Extend the wrapper to parse more fields of each JSON result, and alert on runs whose result text mentions a warning. B. Have each run report a confidence score with its result, and review the passing runs that score below 80 percent. C. Keep the current checks, and raise the random sample of passing diffs from three to six each morning. D. Keep the current checks, and draw the sample of passing diffs from each repository type, recording errors per type.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: D. Option D is correct. Both bad runs passed the automated checks and both came from the four Python repositories, so the errors sit in a segment that a uniform sample of three misses on most mornings and that a figure of 29 passing runs conceals. Sampling within each repository type puts a Python diff in front of a reviewer each morning and gives an error rate per type rather than one aggregate number. Option A leans further on exit codes and JSON results, which are the right first filter for failed runs, but these runs reported success. Option B routes review by self-reported confidence that has not been calibrated against known outcomes, and a run that pins a wrong version reports success with confidence. Option C is the existing process with twice the effort: the sample stays uniform, so most of it lands on TypeScript repositories. Domain 5 (Context Management & Reliability) · Task 5.5 References: • Run Claude Code programmatically — Basic usage • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Fan out across files

fields.Front:
Your automation pipeline has one Claude instance implement a change from an issue, and a separate fresh instance review the resulting pull request. The review run receives the diff and nothing else. Twice this month it approved a change that compiled and read cleanly but left out one of the acceptance criteria listed in the issue. A teammate proposes passing the issue text and its acceptance criteria into the review run alongside the diff. Another engineer objects that the reviewer was deliberately given a clean context.

How should you respond to the proposal?

A. Reject it, because a reviewer unaware of how the change was built is the one that judges the diff on its merits.
B. Accept it, because the criteria define what the diff is checked against and are not the implementer's reasoning.
C. Accept it, and add the implementer's session transcript, because it shows how each criterion was dealt with.
D. Reject it, because the implementing run should confirm each criterion itself before opening the pull request.
fields.Back: Correct Answer: B. Option B is correct. Independence means the reviewer does not inherit the reasoning that produced the change; it does not mean reviewing without a standard. The acceptance criteria are the specification the diff has to meet, and a reviewer that receives only the diff has no way to notice that a required behavior is absent, which is the miss described. Option A applies a sound principle to the wrong input: a session transcript would carry the implementer's reasoning, but the issue and its criteria say nothing about how the change was built. Option C closes the gap and gives the benefit away, because the transcript brings the implementer's justifications into the review. Option D is self-review in the generating session, where the run that overlooked a criterion is the least likely to question the omission, and the reviewer would be left unable to check it. Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering & Structured Output) · Task 4.6 References: • Best practices for Claude Code — Add an adversarial review step • Best practices for Claude Code — Run multiple Claude sessions
